name: Rear naked choke

primary_target.mechanism: Bilateral compression of the carotid arteries and jugular veins between the attacker's biceps and forearm (elbow crease centred under the chin), with the second hand behind the head driving the head forward into the crook; cerebral hypoperfusion plus baroreceptor-mediated vasodilation causes unconsciousness in roughly 9-10 s if held
primary_target.plain: Squeezes the arteries and veins on both sides of the neck between your biceps and forearm, cutting blood flow to the brain — a blood choke, not a windpipe choke. Held, it puts them to sleep in about ten seconds.

secondary_targets.mechanism: Second hand/forearm behind the head pushes it forward into the choking arm
secondary_targets.plain: Your other hand behind their head pushes it forward into the choking arm.

positions.note: Classic finish from hooks + seat belt; Ribeiro teaches it as the primary back attack
From the back of turtle before hooks are in
Standing rear clinch / self-defence

ibjjf.note: Legal in every IBJJF division (not listed in the 6.2.3-M illegal-moves table). 6.2.3-I: strangling without the gi using one or both hands around the neck, or pressing the windpipe with the thumb, is a severe foul (DQ); 6.2.3-J: blocking nose/mouth with the hands is a severe foul.

summary: Arm encircles the neck from behind, hand on own biceps, other hand behind the head; squeeze to shut off the arteries on both sides of the neck. The highest-percentage submission in BJJ and MMA.

sources.locator: Ch. 6-8 (ground fighting, winning from the top)

notes: Physiology literature (Mitchell 2012; Int J Neurosci review) says carotid compression, jugular compression and carotid baroreceptor stimulation all contribute; it is not purely arterial occlusion.

name: Guillotine choke

primary_target.mechanism: Forearm/wrist blade is drawn up and across the front of the neck while the attacker's chest and the opponent's own shoulder close the other side; the high-elbow version angles the forearm onto the carotids (blood choke), the standard version compresses the trachea as well (air + blood)
primary_target.plain: Your forearm pulls up across the front of the neck while your chest and their own shoulder close the other side. The high-elbow version squeezes the arteries on the side of the neck (blood choke); the standard version also crushes the windpipe (air and blood).

secondary_targets.mechanism: Head is pulled down into forward flexion by the front headlock before the squeeze
secondary_targets.plain: The front headlock bends their head and neck forward and down before you squeeze.

positions.note: From a sprawl / snap-down; Danaher's front headlock system treats it as the primary finish
Pull guard with the head trapped; squeeze while legs control posture
Counter to a low shot or a head-down clinch
Marcelotine / arm-in entries when opponent's head drops

ibjjf.note: Row 5 'Frontal guillotine choke' is illegal for 4-12 and 13-15 y.o. only; legal from 16 y.o./white belt in gi and no-gi. Row 2 'Choke with spinal lock' (crank-heavy guillotines) is legal from 16 y.o. too.

summary: Front headlock choke: wrap the neck from the front, grip your own hand or biceps, and squeeze upward while controlling the opponent's posture. Marcelo Garcia and Danaher popularised the high-elbow variant.
notes: Blood vs air split depends on forearm placement; coaching sources agree the high-elbow version is primarily carotid and the low 'wrist in the throat' version is primarily tracheal.

name: Arm-in guillotine

primary_target.mechanism: One of the opponent's arms is trapped inside the headlock; the forearm compresses one carotid/trachea while the opponent's own trapped shoulder closes the other side, similar to an arm triangle mechanism
primary_target.plain: With one of their arms trapped inside, your forearm squeezes one side of the neck (artery or windpipe) while their own shoulder squeezes the other side — like an arm triangle.

secondary_targets.mechanism: Opponent's own shoulder is driven into the neck
secondary_targets.plain: Their own trapped shoulder is driven into the side of their neck.

positions.note: Arises when the opponent's arm is inside the headlock after a sprawl
Finish from guard with elbows tight and hips driven in
Common when the passer's head drops low

ibjjf.note: Covered by rows 5 (frontal guillotine) and 8 (arm triangle): illegal under 16 only.

summary: A guillotine where the opponent's arm is trapped inside the choke; relies on the opponent's own shoulder to close the far side of the neck.
notes: Mechanism description taken from coaching sources, not textbooks.

name: Triangle choke

primary_target.mechanism: Head and one arm are enclosed in a figure-four of the attacker's legs; the thigh/hamstring compresses one carotid and the opponent's own trapped shoulder compresses the other as the legs squeeze and the head is pulled down
primary_target.plain: Your legs lock around their head and one arm: your thigh squeezes the artery on one side of the neck and their own trapped shoulder squeezes the other, cutting blood flow to the brain.

secondary_targets.mechanism: Pulling the head into flexion tightens the choke (a crank element if the choke is not on)
secondary_targets.plain: Pulling their head down bends the neck forward and tightens the choke — it becomes a neck crank if the choke is not on.

secondary_targets.mechanism: Arm is pulled across the neck to close the far side
secondary_targets.plain: Their trapped arm is pulled across the neck to close the far side.

positions.note: Fundamental guard submission; Ribeiro/Renzo both teach it from closed guard
Spider/lasso/butterfly entries
Bravo's rubber guard flows into the triangle
Mounted triangle / from S-mount
Rear triangle (ushiro sankaku) variant

ibjjf.note: Row 7 'Triangle (pulling head)' illegal only for 4-12 and 13-15 y.o.; the triangle itself is legal in all divisions. Row 1 'stretching legs apart' is unrelated.

summary: Legs form a figure-four around the opponent's neck and one arm; squeeze the knees and pull the head to shut off the arteries on both sides of the neck.

sources.locator: Ch. 7 Winning From the Bottom Position

name: Arm triangle choke

primary_target.mechanism: Attacker's arm wraps the neck while the opponent's own arm/shoulder is pinned across the other side; attacker's shoulder and biceps compress one carotid, the trapped shoulder compresses the other
primary_target.plain: Your arm wraps the neck and pins their own arm and shoulder against it: your shoulder and biceps squeeze the artery on one side of the neck, their trapped shoulder squeezes the other — a blood choke.

secondary_targets.mechanism: Driven into the neck
secondary_targets.plain: Their own shoulder is driven into the side of their neck.

positions.note: Trap the arm across, dismount to the side, walk hips toward the head
Kesa-gatame / head-and-arm pressure finish
Very common from top half guard when the underhook is beaten
Less common bottom version

ibjjf.note: Row 8 'Arm triangle' is illegal for 4-12 and 13-15 y.o. only.

summary: Head-and-arm strangle: one arm around the neck, the opponent's arm trapped against their own neck, finished by squeezing and walking the hips.
notes: Wikipedia cites a 7.2 s mean time to unconsciousness for the standard version (Stellpflug et al.).

name: D'Arce choke

primary_target.mechanism: Arm-triangle variant: choking arm threads under the opponent's near arm, across the front of the neck and on top of the far arm, gripping own biceps; forearm compresses one carotid and the trapped shoulder the other
primary_target.plain: A type of arm triangle: your arm threads under their near arm and across the front of the neck; your forearm squeezes the artery on one side and their trapped shoulder the other.

secondary_targets.mechanism: Pinned into the neck by the attacker's chest
secondary_targets.plain: Their near shoulder is pinned into their own neck by your chest.

positions.note: From sprawl/turtle when the opponent's arm is inside
Classic entry when the bottom player's underhook arm is exposed
When opponent turns in with the arm extended
Thread under the near arm from the side

ibjjf.note: Treated as an arm triangle (row 8): illegal under 16 only.

summary: Arm-in choke threaded under the near arm and over the far arm; named for Joe D'Arce, popularised in no-gi.

name: Anaconda choke

primary_target.mechanism: From the front headlock, choking arm passes under the neck and outside the near arm, gripping own biceps; the attacker rolls the opponent onto the trapped shoulder so shoulder and biceps close both carotids
primary_target.plain: From the front headlock, your arm goes under the neck and around their arm; rolling them onto the trapped shoulder lets that shoulder and your biceps squeeze the arteries on both sides of the neck.

secondary_targets.mechanism: Opponent is rolled onto the trapped shoulder (gator roll) to tighten
secondary_targets.plain: Rolling them onto their trapped shoulder (the gator roll) tightens the choke.

positions.note: Primary entry after a sprawl; Danaher dedicates a volume to it
Against a turtled opponent

ibjjf.note: Arm triangle family (row 8): illegal under 16 only.

summary: Front-headlock arm triangle with the arm under the neck and outside the opponent's arm, finished by rolling them onto the trapped shoulder.

name: North-south choke

primary_target.mechanism: From north-south the attacker's arm wraps the neck, elbow on the mat, and the attacker's biceps/shoulder and chest drop onto the neck; carotids are compressed between the arm and the attacker's torso — a body-weight blood choke rather than a squeeze
primary_target.plain: Your arm wraps the neck and your biceps, shoulder and chest sink onto it, squeezing the arteries on the side of the neck between your arm and your body — a body-weight blood choke rather than an arm squeeze.

positions.note: Marcelo Garcia's signature; set up when opponent turns in from side control
Transition from side control as the opponent pushes

ibjjf.note: Not in the illegal-moves table; legal in all divisions.

summary: Arm around the neck from north-south, finish by sinking the shoulder and walking the hips toward the head rather than squeezing.
notes: Marcelo Garcia's 2011 book does not clearly include this choke; sourced from his instructional descriptions instead.

name: Cross collar choke

primary_target.mechanism: Both hands grip deep in opposite collars so the forearms cross in an X across the neck; pulling the elbows down/in drives the radial edges of the forearms and the collar into both carotids
primary_target.plain: Your hands grip deep in opposite collars so your forearms cross over the neck; pulling the elbows down drives the thumb-side edge of your forearms and the collar into the arteries on both sides of the neck.

positions.note: Roger Gracie's signature; first grip deep behind the neck, drop the head
The first submission taught in most gi curricula
Grips set while the opponent frames
Top half guard variant

ibjjf.note: Gi only (requires collars). Legal in all divisions. 6.2.2-S: using an untied belt to assist a choke is a penalty.

summary: Classic gi strangle: cross grips on the collars, pull the elbows to the ribs so the collar and forearms squeeze the arteries on both sides of the neck.

name: Sliding collar choke

primary_target.mechanism: From behind, one hand slides the far lapel across the front of the throat while the other hand pulls the near lapel down; the collar tightens like a noose across both carotids
primary_target.plain: From behind, one hand slides their lapel across the front of the throat while the other pulls the other lapel down, so the collar tightens like a noose over the arteries on both sides of the neck.

positions.note: Primary gi choke from the back; precursor of the bow-and-arrow
Feed the lapel before the opponent recovers guard

ibjjf.note: Gi only; legal in all divisions.

summary: One of the Kodokan's twelve shime-waza: slide one lapel across the neck from behind and pull the other down.

name: Bow and arrow choke

primary_target.mechanism: Deep collar grip across the neck from the back while the other hand controls the far pant leg; the attacker extends the body like drawing a bow so the collar cuts across both carotids with full-body leverage
primary_target.plain: A deep collar grip across the neck is pulled tight as you stretch your body out like drawing a bow, so the collar cuts across the arteries on both sides of the neck with whole-body leverage.

secondary_targets.mechanism: Leg is pulled to stretch the opponent and prevent them turning
secondary_targets.plain: Pulling their far leg by the trousers stretches them out and stops them turning to escape.

positions.note: The highest-percentage gi finish from the back; Ribeiro teaches it as the back's main collar attack
From the clock-choke setup, pull the leg and roll

ibjjf.note: Gi only; legal in all divisions.

summary: Back-control collar choke finished by gripping the far leg and extending the body like a bow; the most common gi choke in modern competition.

name: Clock choke

primary_target.mechanism: Against a turtled opponent the attacker takes a deep collar grip across the neck, drops chest weight on the upper back and walks the feet around the head like a clock hand; the collar and the attacker's weight compress the carotids
primary_target.plain: A deep collar grip across the neck plus your chest weight on their upper back, as you walk around their head, squeezes the arteries on the side of the neck with the collar.

positions.note: Rear knee blocks the gap between opponent's elbow and knee; walk toward the head

ibjjf.note: Gi only; legal in all divisions.

summary: Turtle-position lapel choke finished by walking around the opponent's head with body weight on the collar grip.

name: Loop choke

primary_target.mechanism: A shallow cross-collar grip is looped over the opponent's head as the head is snapped down; the forearm passes over the neck and the free hand behind the head closes the loop so the collar cuts into both carotids
primary_target.plain: A collar grip is looped over their lowered head; your forearm goes over the neck and your free hand behind the head closes the loop so the collar cuts into the arteries on both sides of the neck.

secondary_targets.mechanism: Head is pushed down and under the looping arm
secondary_targets.plain: Their head is pushed down and under your looping arm.

positions.note: After a sprawl or snap-down
Classic entry when the passer's head is low
Against a passer driving forward
Seated guard loop choke

ibjjf.note: Gi only; legal in all divisions.

summary: Collar grip looped over the opponent's lowered head; the arm wraps and rolls to tighten the lapel across the arteries on the side of the neck.
notes: Sources are coaching blogs; judo naming is inconsistent.

name: Ezekiel choke

primary_target.mechanism: One arm wraps behind the head and grips inside the other sleeve; the free forearm/fist passes across the front of the neck and the two arms scissor, compressing carotids and (depending on placement) the trachea
primary_target.plain: One arm goes behind their head gripping your other sleeve; your free forearm crosses the front of the neck and the two arms scissor together, squeezing the arteries on the side of the neck and, depending on placement, the windpipe.

positions.note: Standard application; Ribeiro covers it in mount submissions
Legal and effective from inside guard
Top half guard
Occasional

ibjjf.note: Row 4 'Forearm choke using the sleeve (Ezequiel choke)' is illegal only for 4-12 and 13-15 y.o.; legal from 16/white up. No-gi version (fist-to-forearm) is also legal for adults.

summary: Sleeve-gripping forearm scissor choke named after judoka Ezequiel Paraguassu; works from mount or even from inside the guard.

name: Baseball bat choke

primary_target.mechanism: Stacked collar grips (one palm up, one palm down like holding a bat); the attacker spins toward north-south, driving chest weight so the forearms and collar close across both carotids and the windpipe
primary_target.plain: With stacked collar grips like holding a bat, you spin toward their head and drive your chest weight so your forearms and the collar close across the arteries on both sides of the neck and the windpipe.

positions.note: Classic setup: grips set from KOB, then spin to north-south
From kesa-gatame style control
Bottom variant (Magid Hage)

ibjjf.note: Gi only; legal in all divisions.

summary: Stacked bat-style collar grips finished by spinning to north-south; famous late-tap choke.
notes: Single instructional source; textbook locator not found.

name: Paper cutter choke

primary_target.mechanism: One hand feeds and pulls the far collar from under the head; the other forearm drops like a blade across the front/side of the neck and drives down into the mat, compressing carotid and windpipe against the lapel
primary_target.plain: One hand pulls their far collar from behind the head while your other forearm cuts down across the front and side of the neck like a blade, squeezing the artery and the windpipe against the lapel.

positions.note: Side control / kesa gatame; also from north-south transition
Collar grip set from KOB

ibjjf.note: Gi only; legal in all divisions. Coaching sources disagree whether it is primarily blood or air.

summary: Side-control lapel choke: pull the collar from behind the head and cut the forearm across the throat.
notes: Blood vs air classification contested in sources.

name: Peruvian necktie

primary_target.mechanism: From the front headlock the attacker locks hands around head and near arm, sits beside the opponent and throws one leg over the back of the neck and the other over the back; extending the legs drives the head down onto the choking wrist, compressing the carotids while forcing cervical flexion
primary_target.plain: With your arms locked around their head and arm, your legs go over their neck and back; straightening your legs drives their head down onto your wrist, squeezing the arteries on the side of the neck while bending the neck forward.

secondary_targets.mechanism: Leg over the neck forces forward flexion (crank component)
secondary_targets.plain: Your leg over the back of the neck forces it to bend forward — a neck crank element.

positions.note: Against a turtled/sprawled opponent
Sit through beside the turtle

ibjjf.note: Classified as a choke with spinal lock (row 2): legal from 16 y.o./white; illegal 4-15. Note the IJF (judo) banned the gi variant in 2022.

summary: Front-headlock choke-crank where the legs go over the neck and back and the body extends; both a strangle and a forward neck crank.
notes: Whether a given application is a 'choke with spinal lock' or a pure crank is a referee judgement.

name: Japanese necktie

primary_target.mechanism: From a failed D'Arce the arm goes over the neck with the hand on the far shoulder, the other hand locks the grip; the attacker drops to the hip and folds the head down, compressing the carotids between forearm and the opponent's trapped shoulder while flexing the neck
primary_target.plain: Your forearm goes over the neck to their far shoulder and you fold their head down: the arteries on the side of the neck are squeezed between your forearm and their own trapped shoulder while the neck is bent forward.

secondary_targets.mechanism: Forward flexion of the head (crank component)
secondary_targets.plain: Folding the head down bends the neck forward — a neck crank element.

positions.note: Follow-up when the D'Arce stalls
Lachlan Giles demonstrates it from top half guard
Against a turtled opponent

ibjjf.note: Choke with spinal lock (row 2): legal from 16/white, illegal 4-15; widely described as a grey area that depends on the referee.

summary: D'Arce cousin finished by folding the opponent's head down over your own forearm; a hybrid choke/crank.

sources.locator: Eddie Bravo quoted calling it a grey area

name: Von Flue choke

primary_target.mechanism: Counter to a guillotine: the attacker passes to side control on the opposite side of the opponent's head while the opponent keeps the guillotine grip; the attacker's shoulder drives into one side of the neck and the opponent's own trapped arm closes the other — a shoulder-compression arm triangle
primary_target.plain: When they hold a guillotine after you pass, your shoulder drives into one side of their neck and their own trapped arm closes the other — a shoulder-pressure arm triangle.

secondary_targets.mechanism: Their own arm becomes the far-side compression
secondary_targets.plain: Their own choking arm becomes the pressure on the far side of their neck.

positions.note: Only arises when the bottom player holds a guillotine after being passed

ibjjf.note: A shoulder choke (arm-triangle family, row 8): illegal under 16 only.

summary: Named after Jason Von Flue; punishes a held guillotine by driving the shoulder into the neck from side control.

name: Buggy choke

primary_target.mechanism: From bottom side control the defender throws the far leg over the top player's head/neck and locks the same-side arm under the knee (figure-four of arm and leg); the head and one arm are trapped so the thigh and the opponent's shoulder compress both carotids, as in a triangle
primary_target.plain: From underneath, your leg goes over their head and your arm locks under your knee, trapping their head and one arm; your thigh and their own shoulder squeeze the arteries on both sides of the neck, as in a triangle.

positions.note: Attacks the top player's head when they stay chest-to-chest with the far arm exposed
Also hit from bottom of turtle/kesa gatame

ibjjf.note: Not in the illegal-moves table; a pure strangle, so legal in all adult divisions. Mostly a no-gi competition technique.

summary: Bottom-side-control strangle: leg over the opponent's head, arm locked under the leg, squeeze.
notes: Sources differ on the exact arm/leg path; no textbook treatment (it is a 2010s-era technique).

name: Gogoplata

primary_target.mechanism: From rubber guard / omoplata setup the shin or instep is placed across the front of the throat; pulling the head down onto the shin compresses the windpipe and carotids
primary_target.plain: Your shin or the top of your foot goes across the front of their throat; pulling their head down onto the shin crushes the windpipe and squeezes the arteries on the side of the neck.

secondary_targets.mechanism: Hands pull the head down onto the shin
secondary_targets.plain: Your hands pull the back of their head down onto your shin.

positions.note: Bravo's rubber guard finish; locoplata uses the free foot to push the choking foot
From a high guard / omoplata position
Mounted gogoplata variant

ibjjf.note: Not listed in the 6.2.3-M table; legal in all adult divisions. 6.2.2-R (foot in the lapel behind the neck) is a separate penalty in the gi.

summary: Shin-across-the-throat choke from the rubber guard, popularised by Eddie Bravo and Nick Diaz.
notes: Primarily tracheal in most descriptions; legality inferred from absence in the official table and fan tables that mark it legal.

name: Crucifix choke

primary_target.mechanism: From the back-control crucifix (one of the opponent's arms trapped between the attacker's legs, the other controlled by the attacker's arm) the free arm wraps the neck, or feeds a lapel, and the attacker extends to strangle
primary_target.plain: With both their arms trapped (one between your legs, one by your arm), your free arm wraps the neck or feeds a lapel and you lean back to strangle.

positions.note: Reached from the turtle / failed single leg; Kesting's 'traditional crucifix'
Entry position

ibjjf.note: Choke from the crucifix is legal at all levels (only the neck-crank 'cattle catch' is prohibited under row 22).

summary: Strangle from the crucifix back-control position with both of the opponent's arms trapped.

name: Short choke

primary_target.mechanism: Variation of the rear naked choke when the arm cannot reach the biceps: the choking hand is gripped by the other hand (palm-to-palm or wrist) and the forearm is pulled into the side of the neck while the head is pinned; compresses the carotids but frequently loads the jaw and cervical spine
primary_target.plain: A rear choke with your hands locked together instead of the biceps grip: your forearm is pulled into the side of the neck and squeezes the arteries, but it often presses on the jaw and cranks the neck too.

secondary_targets.mechanism: Forearm across jaw and pulling adds a crank element
secondary_targets.plain: Your forearm across the jaw, and pulling, add a neck crank element.

positions.note: When the opponent hides the chin and denies the full RNC
From the back of a turtled opponent

ibjjf.note: Legal as a choke; if the referee judges it a jaw/neck crank without strangle it falls under row 22 (illegal everywhere).

summary: Shallow rear choke with the hands locked instead of the biceps grip; effective but crank-prone.
notes: Terminology ('short choke' vs 'power half') is inconsistent across sources; mechanism partly inferred.

name: Can opener
aliases: Neck crank from inside the guard

structures: cervical spine (C-spine facet joints, posterior ligaments)
primary_target.mechanism: From inside the closed guard the top player clasps both hands behind the opponent's head and pulls it into forced forward flexion toward the chest while driving the hips forward
primary_target.plain: From inside their guard you clasp both hands behind their head and pull it forward towards their chest, forcibly bending the neck forward — a neck crank, not a choke.

positions.note: Historically used to open the guard; now a pure crank

ibjjf.note: Row 22 'Spinal lock without choke': illegal in every division (kids through adult brown/black no-gi).

summary: Pulling the opponent's head forward from inside their guard; a forward neck crank banned in IBJJF at every level.

name: North-south neck crank

primary_target.mechanism: Arms clasp the head from north-south or kesa gatame and lift/rotate it against the fixed shoulders, forcing cervical flexion or lateral flexion without any carotid compression
primary_target.plain: Your arms clasp their head and lift or twist it while their shoulders are pinned, bending the neck forward or sideways — a neck crank with no choke on the arteries.

positions.note: Lift the head while the chest pins the torso
Kesa gatame head crank

ibjjf.note: Row 22 'Spinal lock without choke': illegal in every division.

summary: Lifting or twisting the pinned opponent's head from north-south; illegal in IBJJF, seen in catch wrestling and MMA.
notes: Generic neck crank; many variants exist.

name: Crucifix neck crank

primary_target.mechanism: Opponent's arms are held out (one between the attacker's legs, one under the arm) while the attacker, facing away, sits back and forces the head into flexion/extension against the trapped shoulders
primary_target.plain: With both their arms trapped and spread, you sit back and force the head to bend forward or back against their pinned shoulders — a neck crank.

secondary_targets.mechanism: Arms are spread to immobilise the shoulder girdle
secondary_targets.plain: Spreading both arms locks their shoulders in place.

positions.note: The 'other' crucifix (Kesting); legal only in no-gi submission wrestling / MMA

ibjjf.note: Row 22 'Spinal lock without choke': illegal in every division. ADCC also forbids the crucifix neck crank.

summary: Catch-wrestling crucifix crank with both arms spread; illegal in BJJ competition.

name: Twister

primary_target.mechanism: Hips are fixed by a leg hook (truck position) while the attacker pulls the opponent's head laterally toward the opposite shoulder with the opponent's arm trapped behind their own head; produces lateral flexion plus rotation of the cervical/thoracic spine
primary_target.plain: With their hips pinned by your leg, you pull their head sideways toward the opposite shoulder, bending and twisting the neck and upper spine sideways at the same time.

secondary_targets.mechanism: Lateral flexion and rotation through the whole spine
secondary_targets.plain: The sideways bend and twist runs through the whole spine, down to the lower back and the sides of the belly.

secondary_targets.mechanism: Arm pinned behind the head
secondary_targets.plain: Their arm is pinned behind their own head.

positions.note: From the 'truck' (one leg hooked) when the back take is incomplete
Truck entry from the turtle

ibjjf.note: Row 22 'Spinal lock without choke': illegal in every division. Legal under ADCC/EBI/MMA (Chan Sung Jung vs Garcia, UFC 2011).

summary: Eddie Bravo's spinal lock from the truck: legs pin the hips while the head is pulled sideways; illegal in IBJJF.

name: Boston crab

structures: lumbar spine (facet joints, anterior longitudinal ligament)
primary_target.mechanism: Opponent face-down; attacker holds both legs under the arms and sits back on the lumbar region, forcing lumbar hyperextension
primary_target.plain: With them face-down, you hold both legs under your arms and sit back on their lower back, bending the lower back backwards past its limit.

secondary_targets.mechanism: Hip hyperextension
secondary_targets.plain: The hips are also bent backwards past their limit.

positions.note: Attacker standing/sitting over a prone opponent; arises from leg-entanglement scrambles

ibjjf.note: Row 22 'Spinal lock without choke': illegal in every division.

summary: Pro-wrestling-derived lock that bends the lower back backwards; a pure spinal lock and illegal under IBJJF rules.
notes: Rare in BJJ; included for completeness of spinal locks.

name: Closed-guard rib/kidney compression

primary_target.mechanism: Bottom player locks the ankles and squeezes the knees/thighs around the torso, compressing the lower ribs and flank
primary_target.plain: From closed guard you lock your ankles and squeeze your knees and thighs around their body, crushing the lower ribs and the side of the belly.

secondary_targets.mechanism: Rib compression
secondary_targets.plain: Squeezes the ribs.

positions.note: Squeezing the legs as a submission (do-jime in judo)

ibjjf.note: Row 9 'Lock inside the closed guard with legs compressing kidneys or ribs': illegal for 4-12, 13-15, 16-17 and adult white belts; legal from blue belt (adult) in gi and no-gi.

summary: Squeezing the opponent's ribs with the closed guard; banned in judo and for IBJJF white belts.
notes: Mechanism is straightforward; included because it is the only torso-compression entry in the IBJJF table.

name: Cross-face

primary_target.mechanism: Attacker's forearm or shoulder is driven across the opponent's jaw/face, turning the head away from the attacker; where the head goes the spine follows, so hip movement and bridging are shut down
primary_target.plain: Your forearm or shoulder drives across their jaw and face, turning the head away from you; where the head goes the spine follows, so they cannot bridge or move their hips.

secondary_targets.mechanism: Forced rotation/lateral flexion
secondary_targets.plain: Forces the neck to twist and bend to the side.

positions.note: The standard side-control head control (Ribeiro)
Cross-face + underhook is the core top half-guard control
Low mount cross-face
Wrestling-style cross-face to break down the turtle

ibjjf.note: Legal; must not become a neck crank (row 22) or hand pressure on the windpipe (6.2.3-I).

summary: Forearm/shoulder across the face turns the opponent's head away, killing their ability to turn in or bridge.

sources.locator: Survival / Guard passing chapters (side control pressure)

name: Head-and-arm control

primary_target.mechanism: One arm encircles the head and neck while the other controls the near arm; the attacker's hip and ribs pin the chest, leaving the opponent flat with the head immobilised
primary_target.plain: One arm wraps their head and neck, the other traps their near arm, and your hip and ribs pin their chest, keeping them flat with the head locked in place.

secondary_targets.mechanism: Hip and body weight on the chest
secondary_targets.plain: Your hip and body weight sit on their chest.

secondary_targets.mechanism: Arm trapped under the attacker's armpit
secondary_targets.plain: Their near arm is trapped under your armpit.

positions.note: Judo kesa gatame; precursor to arm triangle, paper cutter, americana
Transition hold

ibjjf.note: Legal pin; side control scores no points but can score an advantage/guard-pass points.

summary: Classic scarf hold: arm around the head, near arm trapped, hips pinning the chest.

sources.locator: Ch. 8 Winning From the Top Position

name: Chin strap

primary_target.mechanism: Hand cups the chin from the front headlock (or from side control) so the head cannot turn or lift; the elbow is kept tight to block posture, setting up guillotines, D'Arce and back takes
primary_target.plain: Your hand cups their chin from the front headlock or side control so the head cannot turn or lift; your tight elbow stops them posturing up.

secondary_targets.mechanism: Head held in flexion
secondary_targets.plain: Holds their head bent forward and down.

positions.note: First grip of Danaher's front headlock system
Chin strap sets up head-and-arm chokes and prevents turning in
After a snap-down

ibjjf.note: Legal; hand must not grip the throat/windpipe (6.2.3-I).

summary: Hand under the chin controlling the head from the front headlock; the entry to guillotine family attacks.

name: Front headlock

primary_target.mechanism: Attacker wraps the opponent's head and one arm from the front after a sprawl or snap-down, chest weight on the back of the neck forcing flexion; controls the head to prevent shots and set up guillotine, anaconda, D'Arce and back takes
primary_target.plain: You wrap their head and one arm from the front and put chest weight on the back of the neck, bending it forward so they cannot shoot or posture up.

secondary_targets.mechanism: Arm controlled at the elbow/triceps
secondary_targets.plain: Their arm is controlled at the elbow and back of the upper arm.

positions.note: The position itself
Against turtle
After sprawling on a shot

ibjjf.note: Legal control; pulling the head down with no choke can be ruled a spinal lock (row 22) if applied as a submission.

summary: Head-and-arm control from the front, hub of the guillotine/D'Arce/anaconda system.

name: Collar tie

primary_target.mechanism: Hand cups the back of the neck with the forearm on the chest; pulling down forces the opponent's head and posture forward, enabling snap-downs, duck-unders and shots
primary_target.plain: Your hand cups the back of their neck with your forearm on their chest; pulling down drags their head and posture forward.

secondary_targets.mechanism: Head pulled down
secondary_targets.plain: Pulls their head down.

positions.note: Wrestling clinch control; in the gi, the collar grip plays the same role

ibjjf.note: Legal.

summary: Hand behind the neck in the standing clinch to break posture and control the head.

name: Overhook

primary_target.mechanism: Attacker's arm wraps over the opponent's arm and clamps it to the ribs, controlling the shoulder and torso; used to stop underhooks, break posture in guard and set up chokes
primary_target.plain: Your arm wraps over their arm and clamps it to their ribs, controlling the shoulder and upper body.

secondary_targets.mechanism: Arm clamped against the torso
secondary_targets.plain: Their arm is clamped against their own body.

positions.note: Overhook guard: setups for triangles, omoplata and loop/brabo chokes
Whizzer counters a single leg or underhook
Whizzer to kill the bottom underhook

ibjjf.note: Legal.

summary: Arm over the opponent's arm clamping it to the torso; the counter to the underhook.
notes: Primary target is arguably shoulder; listed here because it is a torso control.

name: Seat belt

primary_target.mechanism: One arm over the opponent's shoulder and the other under the opposite armpit, hands clasped on the chest; locks the attacker's chest to the opponent's back and controls the upper body, the standard precursor to the rear naked choke
primary_target.plain: One arm over their shoulder and one under the opposite armpit, hands clasped on their chest, locks your chest to their back and controls the upper body.

secondary_targets.mechanism: Shoulder line controlled
secondary_targets.plain: Controls the line of both shoulders.

positions.note: Core back-control grip (with hooks)
Seat belt before inserting hooks
Rear standing clinch

ibjjf.note: Legal; back control scores 4 points when hooks are in and the position is held 3 s (Art. 4.5).

summary: Over-under chest grip from behind; the foundation of back control.

name: Crucifix control

primary_target.mechanism: From the back/turtle, one of the opponent's arms is trapped between the attacker's legs and the other by the attacker's arm, leaving both arms unable to defend the neck
primary_target.plain: From the back or turtle, one of their arms is trapped between your legs and the other by your arm, so neither arm can defend the neck.

secondary_targets.mechanism: Neck is defenceless
secondary_targets.plain: Leaves the neck open to chokes.

positions.note: Reached from turtle, failed single leg or fireman's carry
Entry

ibjjf.note: Position is legal at all levels; only the neck-crank finish is prohibited.

summary: Back-side control with the opponent's arms spread by legs and arm; sets up collar and arm chokes.

name: Knee on belly

primary_target.mechanism: Top player places the knee or shin on the opponent's belly, chest or ribs with the other foot posted; body weight drives through the knee, restricting breathing and movement while the attacker stays mobile
primary_target.plain: Your knee or shin drives your body weight into their belly, chest or ribs with your other foot posted, making it hard to breathe and move while you stay mobile.

secondary_targets.mechanism: Knee can ride up onto the chest
secondary_targets.plain: Your knee can ride up onto the chest.

positions.note: The position itself; transitions from side control
Entry

ibjjf.note: Legal; Art. 4.3: 2 points when the knee/shin closest to the hip is on the belly, chest or ribs, other knee off the ground, held 3 s with the opponent on back or side.

summary: Knee driven into the belly with the other foot posted: a mobile 2-point pin that drains the opponent and opens collar chokes.

name: Chest-to-chest side control pressure

primary_target.mechanism: Attacker's chest is driven across the opponent's chest with hips low and weight off the knees, compressing the ribcage and limiting breathing; combined with cross-face and underhook to immobilise the shoulders
primary_target.plain: Your chest drives across theirs with your hips low and weight off your knees, crushing the ribs and making it hard to breathe.

secondary_targets.mechanism: Cross-face often added
secondary_targets.plain: A cross-face is often added.

secondary_targets.mechanism: Underhook pins the far shoulder
secondary_targets.plain: An underhook pins their far shoulder.

positions.note: Ribeiro's side-control survival chapter is built around escaping this pressure
Pressure shifts to the chest/face
Low mount chest pressure

ibjjf.note: Legal; passing to side control scores 3 points (guard pass), side control itself scores none.

summary: Heavy chest-on-chest pin from side control; the baseline control every escape chapter begins with.

sources.locator: Ch. 8 Winning From the Top Position

name: Hand-on-throat strangle (illegal)

primary_target.mechanism: Direct squeezing of the throat with one or both hands, thumb pressure on the windpipe, or covering the nose/mouth; closes the airway rather than the carotids
primary_target.plain: Squeezing the throat directly with the hands or thumbs on the windpipe, or covering the nose and mouth; it cuts off the air rather than squeezing the arteries on the side of the neck.

positions.note: Self-defence context only

ibjjf.note: 6.2.3-I: strangling without the gi with one or both hands around the neck, or thumb pressure on the windpipe, is a severe foul (DQ); 6.2.3-J: blocking the nose/mouth with the hands is a severe foul.

summary: Bare-hand throat strangle or smother; explicitly a disqualifying foul in IBJJF competition.
notes: Included so the app can show why hand-on-throat is never an option in sport BJJ.
